title: Almost everything is an expression
summary: Blocks, if, and match produce values; a trailing semicolon throws the value away.
lecture: In Rust, `if`, `match`, and plain `{}` blocks are expressions: they produce values. The last line of a block, written without a semicolon, is the block's value. Add a semicolon and you turn it into a statement whose value is `()`, the unit type.
This is why function bodies usually end with a bare expression instead of `return`. `return` exists for early exits; using it on the last line is redundant, and Clippy's needless_return lint says so.
The most common beginner error in this area is E0308: the function promises `-> i32` but the body ends with a semicolon, so it returns `()`. Delete the semicolon and the types line up.
